"And you are the past." The next attack came with force that made the ground crack under Selphira's feet. 

For the first time in decades, the legendary warrior found herself genuinely outmatched.

Like a bell without a clapper.  "Have you noticed anything strange lately?" Reed asked suddenly, accepting the cup Fern offered him.  "What do you mean?" "With our plants," he explained, extending his arm where the vines gently coiled.  In the lamplight, they seemed to pulse with a subtle emerald glow.  And yesterday, I could lift the water barrel without help.  Fern studied him thoughtfully, absently stroking the leaves that peeked from her collar. 

They felt smoother under her fingers, more vibrant.  "Now that you mention it, I've been sleeping better, and my hair is regaining color.  "Must be that we're sleeping more due to his absence," Reed finally suggested, though uncertainty tinged his voice.  "Or perhaps it's the new herbs we're using in the kitchen." "Yes, that must be it," Fern agreed, though she didn't sound entirely convinced.  Neither wanted to admit it from fear to get ideas and make the absence more painful, but both had begun to wonder if Ren's daily ritual was having some actual effect.  It was absurd, of course.  It was an established fact.  And yet, "I wonder how he's doing at school," Fern said, changing the subject. 

She sipped her tea, savoring its soothing warmth.  Do you think he's made friends?  The restaurant work was stable, at least, and occasionally they received extra tips for their special culinary creations.  Later, as they prepared for bed, Fern paused by the window, gazing at the multiple moons illuminating the night with their subtle colored light.  The smallest moon, crimson as a ruby, peeked from behind a cloud, casting a reddish glow across her face.  I just hope he's all right, she murmured, more to herself than to Reed.  "I have this feeling, you know, that something good is happening with our Wren.  Something unexpected." Fern leaned against him, finding solace in his presence.  After decades together, they still fit perfectly, two pieces of the same puzzle. 

"Perhaps you're right," she said finally.  His thoughts, however, were far from the academy.  They drifted to the small rented house where his parents, Reed and Fern, would probably be sleeping after a long day working in the kitchens.  The image of them, exhausted but determined, faithfully following the ritual he had taught them, made his heart constrict.  He could almost smell the spices that would cling to their clothes, see the flour dusting his father's forearms.

Mr.  Finch's high-pitched, mocking voice sliced through the silence.  The Academyy's most prosperous fungus cultivator.  My most intriguing depositor.  "Good afternoon, Mr.

Finch raised a hand dramatically, found an ancestral treasure, robbed a noble's chest, or perhaps your mushrooms have hallucinogenic properties, and you've been selling them to the senior students.  The mushrooms pulsed with amusement as Ren slid the report across the counter.  What's this?  Finch adjusted his glasses.  Your written confession.  How considerate.  "No, no, there must be a mistake." "Is there a problem?" Ren asked, suppressing a smile.  "Problem?" Finch let out a hysterical laugh.  "The problem is these numbers make no sense.  Two weeks ago, you bring five dark bronze crystals, which was already suspicious enough.  105,000 crystals in total.  Finch removed his glasses to clean them compulsively with a spore.  The weakest recorded creature.  Are you certain you haven't been selling illegal substances?  Ah, yes, the signatures.  Finch narrowed his eyes.  You're sure you didn't forge them?  Or perhaps hypnotize the professors?  Just he says.  Finch turned to his mouse.  Did you hear that, Theodore?  Just 5,000 crystals as if it were pocket change.  Tiny paws moving across the ledger with surprising dexterity.  You know, Finch leaned over the counter, his eyes gleaming with undisguised curiosity.  I've been at this bank for 15 years.  I've seen students with legendary beasts amass fortunes.  Yes.  Finch began counting but paused mid-motion.  Just 5,000.  No grand plans.  Boring.  Finch sighed dramatically.  Sure you won't share your secret.  Between financial colleagues.  Ha, good luck.  Finch snorted while counting crystals.  Next, you'll tell me you want it all playing dice.  As the banker prepared his withdrawal, Ren reflected on his true plans.  The problem was that now they had to rent it. He lived 240 years under my shadow, always Selph'ra's son, never really his own man.  Lionel moved closer, and for the first time in years, Selph'ra saw genuine vulnerability behind his mask of confidence.  Laura had fun, he murmured. 

She found her place.  How had she failed so completely in understanding the needs of someone she loved so much?  War isn't a game, Lionel, she said finally.  It's not an opportunity to win glory.  It's blood, pain, loss.  Laura had died pursuing her dreams.  Lionel was willing to die pursuing his.  When had protection stopped being protection and become prison?  The promise I'm going to fulfill, she said slowly, is personal.  It won't be a battle where you can win easy glory.  Then let me make my own promise, Lionel replied immediately.  Let me find my own battle.  But don't leave me here, waiting once again for someone else to decide when I'm ready to live my life.  I can't promise you glory or recognition.  I can only promise you that you'll have the chance to prove who you really are amid violence and pain without my shadow protecting you." Lionel's eyes lit up with a mixture of triumph and terror.  "It's all I've ever wanted," he said simply.  Selfer nodded slowly, feeling as if she were signing a death sentence, his, hers, or maybe both.  "Then prepare yourself.  We leave in an hour." As Lionel ran off to prepare, Selfer remained alone with her thoughts and the overwhelming weight of a decision she knew she might regret for the rest of her very, very long life.  "If there is a rest of life to regret," she thought grimly. 

Victor soared above the air currents that his giant golden eagle generated effortlessly, his eyes scanning the battlefield with the advantage only an elite aerial tamer like him could obtain.

The group hurried through the widened opening, Lin ensuring that everyone passed safely before her, but also covering for Mira and Matilda to keep the line going as the shadow stalkers surged forward.  In Liora and Luna's group, the last Shadow Stalker was crushed under the power of Julius's Earth Wolverine. "Prince Julius," Luna began, her normally controlled voice now tense with effort and concern.

I won't leave.  Luna could smell her cousins, Leora and Lissa, somewhere nearby.  There was no way she would abandon them.  Harold didn't give them time to argue.  She's not from a rich family," one of the guards shouted, her voice charged with indignation. 

"Lissa is the king's daughter." Ren almost lost control of his light claws.  Cold sweat began running down his back as the pieces clicked into place in his mind.  The connection with Julius, the resemblance he had noticed but ignored.  Taro added, his voice trembling.  Lissa seized the moment to break away from men, running toward where her guards waited.  Once they had her behind them, the agents demeanor changed completely.  Enough games, the Wolverine guard growled, her beast tensing for attack.  His fist, charged with disruptive mana, connected with her stomach.  He couldn't manipulate her flow delicately as he had done with Lissa, but he could cause moderate damage to deny her the capability.  The beastless guard and manalissa tried to attack him from behind, but their punches and kicks bounced uselessly off the hydra's crystallin scales.  "Taro!" Ren shouted while maintaining his position over the other guard.  And in case you haven't noticed, you're not exactly in a position to talk, so you're going to listen.  He approached Lissa, leaning until his eyes, burning with indignation, were inches from hers.  The princess tensed, unaccustomed to anyone invading her personal space so boldly.  "You have a mineral fairy, don't you?" Ren asked, his voice more controlled, but still intense.  "Then, like Luna, you have the perception ability.  You can sense when someone lies through mana flow, too." Lissa's eyes widened in surprise.  It was true. 

Her beast could detect the fluctuations in mana that occurred when someone lied.  But how did he know?  Lissa nodded tentatively.  Then use it, Ren challenged her.  See if I'm lying when I say I have nothing to do with Yo.  Lissa closed her eyes for a moment, her mineral fairy partially manifesting.  The mana fluctuations around Ren were clear.  Crystalline.  Not you nor Luna when I see her with her blue hair spying on me sometimes.  Oh, Lissa interrupted, a small smile forming on her lips.  Actually, Leora is the one who always spies on you.  Luna only watches you during classes.  He's telling the truth.  Lissa cut them off about everything.  She turned to Ren, curiosity sparkling in her eyes.  Why are you here then?

The corridors between stadiums were relatively empty, most students focused already on the highest level battles, the new students or their respective trials.  Liu advanced quickly, his banshee hyena partially manifesting in his legs to enhance his speed even further.  He had carefully studied the matchups.  Fortunately, his turn was the last in his group, giving him this precious window of opportunity.  The stands rose higher, the protective barriers were visibly more robust, and the arena itself showed signs of more intense combat, partially repaired craters, burn marks, and residual crystallizations from previous battles. 

Liu found a seat in the lower stands where younger students typically gathered to observe their seniors.  The stadium was approximately at half capacity with scattered groups of students discussing strategies and analyzing previous battles.  Their conversations were more technical, their gestures more precise as they debated advanced techniques.  He had arrived early, the seventh year battles seemed to take a bit longer.  Liu watched the battle, which fortunately took only 15 minutes.  And finally, Liu's heart accelerated with anticipation.  It was Zhou Liwei's team's turn.  Three seventh year students advanced toward the arena with the characteristic confidence of experienced tamers.  Their uniforms had different colored lines than Liu's and bore silver insignias.  One of them even displayed a gold emblem that caught the light with each movement. 

Zhou Liwei stood out even among his advanced level companions.

"With our plants," he explained, extending his arm where the vines gently coiled.  In the lamplight, they seemed to pulse with a subtle emerald glow.  And that migraine that used to torment me hasn't returned in weeks." They looked at each other in silence, an unspoken question hanging between them like morning mist.  "Must be that we're sleeping more due to his absence," Reed finally suggested, though uncertainty tinged his voice.  "Or perhaps it's the new herbs we're using in the kitchen." "Yes, that must be it," Fern agreed, though she didn't sound entirely convinced.  Neither wanted to admit it from fear to get ideas and make the absence more painful, but both had begun to wonder if Ren's daily ritual was having some actual effect.  Do you think he's made friends?  I'm sure he has, Reed answered, though worry briefly crossed his face, deepening the lines around his eyes.  Although with a spore He didn't need to finish the sentence.  They both knew the stigma associated with Ren's beast, the weakest of all.  Remember the day he left with that determined look in his eyes.  Reed smiled, admiring the conviction in his wife's voice.  Her unwavering faith had always been one of the qualities he loved most about her.  You're right.  The smallest moon, crimson as a ruby, peeked from behind a cloud, casting a reddish glow across her face.  I just hope he's all right, she murmured, more to herself than to Reed.  That he's happy, that he's learning, that he doesn't feel alone.  Reed approached, embracing her from behind.  His arms encircled her waist, strong and comforting.  "He is," he replied softly.  His thoughts, however, were far from the academy.  They drifted to the small rented house where his parents, Reed and Fern, would probably be sleeping after a long day working in the kitchens.  The image of them, exhausted but determined, faithfully following the ritual he had taught them, made his heart constrict.  He could almost smell the spices that would cling to their clothes, see the flour dusting his father's forearms.

It hadn't been malice, simply the natural concern of preserving succession lines that had been involuntarily guarded in her shadow for centuries.  But Selphora had had too much maternal love to give, and Leonel and Laura reminded her so much of her first children that she couldn't help treating them as legitimate heirs.  "The war has begun," she said finally, deciding on partial truth.  "There is a promise I made, a debt that must be paid." Leonel's eyes lit up with a light that Selphora had learned to fear.  "Exactly.  The war." He moved closer, his lesser white serpent manifesting partially in his features, sharpening his face.  That blood doesn't matter.  You promised that, too." Selphora closed her eyes, feeling the weight of every wrong decision she had made during the last decades.  She had lost Laura just 8 years ago.  Her adoptive daughter, her beloved daughter.  The girl who had grown into an intrepid explorer had died along with her husband on one of their adventure trips.  Laura had been born with the strongest will to see the world and had inherited Selphora's love for living to the fullest, the philosophy the long-lived woman had developed after seeing so many people regret, at the end of their lives, not having pursued their dreams.  That philosophy, along with that innate love for exploration and adventure, had been what had finally caused Laura her life.  Selphora had been left in charge of Leora, the small three-year-old granddaughter, and Lionel had become her absolute priority. 

But unlike Laura, who had thirsted for adventures, Lionel thirsted for power.  And Selphora knew it.  She had known it for years.  She constantly found herself in a dilemma that ate at her from within.  Take me to war to earn indisputable merit.  When we return victorious, no one will be able to question my position." "He's already an adult," Selphora reminded herself, but not really.  She had spoiled him, perhaps too much.  Perhaps he had lacked a father figure, someone to set firm limits when she couldn't do it.  Lionel had already grown up, had already been formed under her influence, and the patterns were too established.  Selphora could see it clearly, the subtle arrogance in his posture, the expectation that the world would bend to his desires, the inability to understand why the bold foxes of the family didn't automatically recognize him as leader, and why his selfish desires couldn't be the priority every time.  And she blamed herself for it.  In the end, she was responsible for this outcome.
